summary: Lake Ontario light on Horse Island beside Sackets Harbor, first shown in 1831; the 1870 brick tower stands on an island closed to the public since 1957.

lens.where: installed 1857 (later replaced 1890; the replacement's order is not given in these sources)

structures.type: one-and-a-half-story keeper's dwelling with a tower rising from the roof
structures.note: LighthouseFriends describes the 1831 dwelling; the archive gives 1831 for the quarters and brick, Queen Anne/Italianate style, which may describe a later building

structures.type: square brick tower on limestone foundation
structures.note: Work began August 1870 about 300 yards southeast of the 1831 lighthouse; completed April 1871; raised ten feet in August 1899. LighthouseFriends gives 55.5 ft (16.9 m) afterwards; the archive gives 50 ft (15.2 m) from base to lantern.
Automated light on a metal skeletal tower replaced the lighthouse's function in 1957 (LighthouseFriends); its location on the island is not stated in the sources used here

access.note: Closed to the general public since 1957 (Lighthouse Digest, 2019). Owned by New York State Parks since 2019. Visitors should not land on the island or cross to it.

events.note: Keeper's dwelling with a tower on its roof, built later in 1831 after Congress appropriated $4,000 in March 1831
Year established per the archive; LighthouseFriends describes the light on the dwelling's tower
Fifth-order Fresnel lens installed in the lantern room
New brick tower begun in August 1870 after Congress provided funds on 15 July 1870
New brick tower completed in April 1871 and lit that year
Old lighthouse torn down after the new tower was finished
Worn-out lens replaced with a new one from the general depot (order not given)
Square tower given a ten-foot addition in August 1899; the Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1900 says it was built ten feet higher
British troops landed on Horse Island on 29 May 1813 and forced the militia back across the causeway; the attack on the port failed
Power boat sank after striking rocks near the light on 22 August 1918; keeper George H. Ward went to help its occupants
Tower repaired in July 1919: cracked mortar and damaged bricks removed; tower painted with a waterproofing compound
Oil light changed to acetylene and from fixed to flashing
LighthouseFriends says the light became an automated flashing acetylene light
Schuyler S. Simmons hired in July 1926 as caretaker with the title of lamplighter; LighthouseFriends says he lived on the island and farmed its seventeen acres until his death in 1933
Automated light on a metal skeletal tower took over the lighthouse's function (LighthouseFriends)
Declared excess and sold by the General Services Administration to a private buyer
Island bought by Campaign 1776, a project of the Civil War Trust (24 acres)
New York State Office of Parks, Recreation, and Historic Preservation reported as owner after the purchase was finalized

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1957 first-year entry (Wikidata, Tower 3) describes the metal tower that replaced the lighthouse's function; the first light is 1831 (archive, LighthouseFriends). The brick tower standing today is the 1870-71 tower.
The archive records the station discontinued in 1957 and no longer an active aid to navigation; the 1957 sale and later ownership confirm that the lighthouse was not a working aid after that year.

notes_for_editor: Most of the station history here comes from LighthouseFriends (facts only; copyrighted, so the story paraphrases it) and from the archive's record. Primary Board and Bulletin sources were found for 1900 (tower raised), 1918 (rescue), 1919-20 (repairs) and 1925 (conversion). Not in the local corpus, so not checked: the Board's 1831-1871 reports (the 1831 appropriation, the 1838 Platt report, the 1869 report quoted for dilapidation, the 1870 funds), the 1883 rescue, the 1890 lens replacement and the 1957 sale. Verify these in the originals before publication. The Galloo Island fog-signal recommendation in the 1891 Board report is for Galloo Island, not Horse Island; it is not used. Keepers: the archive gives Holloway from 1884, LighthouseFriends says 1883; LighthouseFriends prints Jacob Kellogg, Jr.; Simmons (lamplighter 1926-1933 per LighthouseFriends and the Digest) is not on the archive roster, which lists James P. Westcott from at least 1939; not reconciled. The 1957 metal skeletal tower's location is not stated here (the record gives 21 m, steel, 1957). Height: LighthouseFriends gives 55.5 ft after the 1899 addition; the archive gives 50 ft from base to lantern; not reconciled. The Bulletin OCR of the 1918 passage is garbled; the story quotes only clean fragments; check the PDF page 43. Newspapers: a Chronicling America search for Horse Island in NY papers 1857-1918 returned West Indies items; Sackets Harbor with lighthouse returned nothing 1883-1930. The Civil War Trust release (2017) and the Digest (2019) are the latest sources; the owner's current access and any rental plans were not checked after 2019. Private residents are not named: the 1957-2017 private owners and the widow of Schuyler Simmons are left out, per the guide's rule for converted lighthouses. Wikipedia is not cited. Fact-check 2026-10-28: 'eastern end of Lake Ontario' removed (the archive says only Lake Ontario); 'with no date set' removed (the Digest says the rental process may take a few years); the 1919 repair passage is attributed to the Lighthouse Service Bulletin (the Bulletin reports it; it does not quote the keeper); the archive roster does not list Simmons and the story now says so. The Lighthouse Digest's 'rentals' and 'trails' are the state's stated plans, not dates.
